title: HTTP-Only Cookies
body:
A [[Cookies|cookie]] set with the `HttpOnly` flag, which tells the browser: **attach this to
requests as normal, but do not let page JavaScript read it.**

```
Set-Cookie: session=a1b2c3; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
```

After that, `document.cookie` simply does not list it. The cookie still goes out on every
matching request, so the server sees no difference at all; the only thing that changed is that
code running in the page cannot get at the value.

The attack it defends against is [[XSS]]. If someone gets a script onto your page, the first
thing that script wants is `document.cookie`, because a session cookie is as good as the
password. `HttpOnly` makes that read return nothing, so a successful XSS still cannot walk off
with the session. It is the reason session tokens belong in an HttpOnly cookie rather than in
[[localStorage]], which page JS can always read.

The three flags travel together and defend different things:

| Flag | Says | Stops |
|---|---|---|
| `HttpOnly` | page JS cannot read it | [[XSS]] stealing the session |
| `Secure` | HTTPS requests only | it being sent in clear text |
| `SameSite` | not on cross-site requests | [[CSRF]] |

One caution about the course-notes framing. The notes introduce these as cookies "only stored
in the browser memory", as a way of not persisting past a restart. That is a real property,
but it is what having **no expiry** gives you, which makes it a [[Session Cookie]]; the two
are independent flags and a cookie can be either, both, or neither. `HttpOnly` is about *who
can read it*, not *how long it lives*.

Flag by flag, with the wristband analogy, in [[Cookies and Browser Storage]]. See
[[Cookie Jar]].
